hints: Look at the products in the equation, a polymer plus $2nHCl$. What does formation of a small molecule alongside the polymer tell you about the polymerisation type?
walkthrough:
Spot the clue in the equation**
Look at the right hand side. You make the polymer plus $2nHCl$. Whenever monomers link and kick out a small molecule such as $HCl$, $H_2O$ or $HCl$, that is the hallmark of condensation, not addition.

Link to monomers**
Here you have two different monomers, a diol $HOROH$ and $COCl_2$, each with two functional groups. They join, $O-H$ plus $C-Cl$ gives $C-O$ link plus $HCl$. Loss of small molecules confirms condensation.
Final answer: Condensation polymerisation, as a small molecule ($HCl$) is eliminated when monomers join.

hints: Start from diol P, remove H from each $OH$ group and join each O to the $C=O$ carbon from $COCl_2$, keeping the whole bisphenol skeleton intact.
walkthrough:
Build from the two monomers**
Think of P as $HO-Ar-C(CH_3)_2-Ar-OH$ where $Ar$ is a para-disubstituted benzene. Each $OH$ loses $H$ and each $Cl$ is lost from $COCl_2$, leaving $O-Ar-C(CH_3)_2-Ar-O-C(=O)-$ to repeat.

Draw it correctly**
Draw $O$ linked to para position of first $C_6H_4$, then central $C(CH_3)_2$, then second para $C_6H_4$, then $O$, then $C(=O)$, then close with continuation bonds outside the bracket and subscript $n$. Do not include $H$ or $Cl$ in the repeat unit.
Final answer: One repeat unit: $[-O-C_6H_4-C(CH_3)_2-C_6H_4-O-C(=O)-]$ with both benzene rings para-disubstituted, continuation bonds through O and C, in brackets with subscript n.

hints: Nalgene has large non-polar aromatic hydrocarbon parts plus polar $C=O$ and $C-O$ carbonate groups, so think which forces arise from temporary versus permanent dipoles.
walkthrough:
Account for the hydrocarbon bulk**
The repeat unit contains two benzene rings and $CH_3$ groups with many electrons. All neighbouring chains can set up temporary dipoles, so London dispersion forces act strongly along the whole chain and give toughness.

Account for the carbonate link**
The $-O-C(=O)-O-$ group is polar because $C=O$ and $C-O$ have permanent dipoles. So permanent dipole-dipole attractions also operate between chains. There is no $O-H$ or $N-H$ left for hydrogen bonding.

Final answer: 1. London (induced dipole-dipole) forces
2. Permanent dipole-dipole forces.

hints: Recall what holds an alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet in shape, which backbone groups ($C=O$ and $N-H$) can hydrogen bond to each other.
Recall what folds the chain in 3D, interactions between side chain R groups rather than the backbone, and name one example such as ionic, disulfide, hydrophobic or van der Waals.
walkthrough:
Separate backbone from side chain**
Picture the protein backbone as a repeating $-CO-NH-$ chain. Secondary structure is the local coiling into helix or sheet. That is held by hydrogen bonds directly between one backbone $C=O$ oxygen and another backbone $H-N$ hydrogen.

Move to 3D folding**
Tertiary structure is the overall 3D folding of that helix or sheet. This is driven by the side chains, the R groups sticking out. R groups can attract by ionic bonds, disulfide $S-S$ bridges, hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic packing and London forces. Naming any one valid R group interaction earns the mark.

Final answer: Secondary structure: stabilised by hydrogen bonding between $C=O$ and $N-H$ groups of the backbone.
Tertiary structure: stabilised by interactions between R groups, e.g. hydrogen bonding, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions, London forces.

hints: Remember the two strands of DNA are held together by hydrogen bonds between bases, not within the sugar phosphate backbone.
Think why only certain pairs fit, A pairs with T and C pairs with G, and how this complementary pairing acts as a template for copying.
walkthrough:
Locate the hydrogen bonds**
The DNA double helix has sugar phosphate backbones on the outside and bases pointing inwards. Hydrogen bonds form between bases on opposite strands, holding the helix together but weak enough to unzip for copying.

Explain specificity for accuracy**
Pairing is highly specific. Adenine $(A)$ hydrogen bonds only to thymine $(T)$, cytosine $(C)$ only to guanine $(G)$, due to size and hydrogen bond donor and acceptor fit. When strands separate, each exposed base picks up only its complement, so the new strand is an exact copy and genetic information is preserved.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonding holds the two strands together between complementary base pairs.
A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so each strand acts as an exact template, ensuring accurate replication of the genetic code.

hints: Think of two different ways to break bonds in the chain, one using water to split polar links like esters or amides, the other using light energy.
walkthrough:
Name two distinct breakdown routes**
Many condensation polymers contain $C-O$ or $C-N$ links that water can split, so hydrolysis with water, acid or alkali degrades them. Separately, high energy UV light can break covalent bonds in the chain, causing photodegradation. These are two different processes.
Final answer: Hydrolysis and degradation by light / UV radiation (photodegradation).

hints: Acid hydrolysis splits every peptide $CO-NH$ link to give free $-CO_2H$ plus $-NH_2$, so look for residues without a side chain and with a $CH_2C_6H_5$ side chain.
Identify the simplest residue ($CH_2$ only between $CO$ and $NH$) as glycine and the benzyl $CH_2$-phenyl residue as phenylalanine, and draw them as $H_2N-CH(R)-CO_2H$.
walkthrough:
Use hydrolysis logic**
Heating with dilute $HCl$ hydrolyses all amide peptide bonds: $-CO-NH- + H_2O \rightarrow -CO_2H + H_2N-$. Apart from threonine given, the diagram shows only two other residue types: $-NH-CH_2-CO-$ with no side chain, and $-NH-CH(CH_2C_6H_5)-CO-$ with a benzyl side chain.

Draw the free amino acids**
The $CH_2$ only residue gives glycine: $H_2N-CH_2-CO_2H$. The benzyl residue gives phenylalanine: $H_2N-CH(CO_2H)-CH_2-C_6H_5$. Draw full displayed or skeletal structures with $NH_2$, central $CH$, $CO_2H$ and for Phe the $CH_2$-phenyl ring.
Final answer: $H_2NCH_2CO_2H$ (glycine, Gly) and $H_2NCH(CH_2C_6H_5)CO_2H$ (phenylalanine, Phe) with $H_2N-CH(CO_2H)-CH_2-$ linked to a benzene ring.

hints: Work round the ring in order, labelling each $-CO-CH(R)-NH-$ unit as Gly where $R = H$, Phe where $R = CH_2C_6H_5$, keeping Thr fixed at the bottom.
walkthrough:
Read round the ring**
Keep Thr fixed at the bottom. Moving round, every $CH_2$ carbonyl to NH unit with no side chain is Gly, every unit with a $CH_2C_6H_5$ side chain is Phe. Following the bonds gives the cyclic sequence Gly, Phe, Phe, Gly, Thr, Phe, Phe and back to the start. Because it is cyclic, the starting point is arbitrary as long as order is preserved.
Final answer: Cyclic order: Gly - Phe - Phe - Gly - Thr - Phe - Phe - (back to Gly), correctly placed round the ring starting from Thr as given.

hints: Recall the two standard A Level methods for separating amino acid mixtures, one based on charge and movement in an electric field, the other based on partitioning on a plate or paper.
walkthrough:
Name charge versus partition methods**
Amino acids differ in charge at a given pH and in solubility and adsorption. So electrophoresis separates them by migration in an electric field, while thin-layer or paper chromatography separates them by different $R_f$ values between stationary and mobile phases.
Final answer: Electrophoresis and thin-layer chromatography / paper chromatography.
